title: Section 139 NI Act — Presumption in favour of holder

content.overview: Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 provides that it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in s. 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. The presumption arises for the holder once the foundational facts of s. 138 are in place. It is rebuttable. The accused may rebut it on a preponderance of probabilities; the section does not require the accused to prove the defence beyond reasonable doubt, and it does not relieve the complainant of the foundational s. 138 facts.
content.study: Do not start with the presumption. First show the s. 138 foundation: cheque, presentation, statutory return, notice and non-payment. Then s. 139 presumes the cheque was received for discharge of a debt or other liability. Rebuttal is on probabilities, by evidence or by pointing to gaps in the complainant's material. The presumption shifts the evidential burden on that issue; it does not create company liability or jurisdiction.

learningObjectives: State the s. 139 presumption and who it favours.
Identify the foundational s. 138 facts that must exist before the presumption is used.
Explain rebuttal on a preponderance of probabilities without raising the defence to proof beyond reasonable doubt.
enhancement.definition: Section 139 presumes, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder received a s. 138 cheque for discharge in whole or in part of any debt or other liability.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The presumption is rebuttable and issue-specific. It concerns the purpose for which the holder received the cheque. It does not prove notice, presentation or jurisdiction.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, s. 139, read with s. 138. Related general cheque presumptions in s. 118 are a different section and are not substituted for s. 139.
essentialIngredients: Cheque of the nature referred to in s. 138
Foundational facts of the s. 138 sequence
Presumption that receipt was for discharge of debt or other liability
Contrary may be proved by the accused
Standard of rebuttal is not the complainant's primary criminal standard
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 139 uses 'shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved'. The subject of the presumption is receipt of the cheque for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. It operates in favour of the holder. A court does not apply it to a stranger who is not the holder, and it does not apply to a cheque outside s. 138. The complainant still has to bring the foundational facts: the cheque, statutory presentation and return, notice and failure to pay. Once those facts are accepted, the accused must lead a probable defence or rely on material already on record that makes the non-existence of a legally enforceable debt reasonably probable. Proof beyond reasonable doubt is not the accused's standard for this rebuttal. A bare denial, without more, is generally not treated as contrary proved, but that evaluative point stays on the case-law gate and is not stated here as a verified holding.
examples: The payee proves the cheque, timely presentation, insufficiency return, notice and non-payment. Section 139 then presumes the cheque discharged a debt.
The drawer produces a probable account that the cheque was issued as a blank security not against any enforceable liability. That is a rebuttal attempt, not a jurisdictional objection.
The complaint omits the statutory notice. Section 139 does not cure the missing s. 138 proviso.
enhancement.problemApplication: Separate foundation from presumption. If a proviso fact is missing, do not reach s. 139. If the foundation is present, ask what probable contrary the accused has proved. Do not use s. 139 to answer s. 141 arraignment or s. 142 forum.
distinctions: Section 139 presumption vs s. 138 foundational facts
Rebuttal on probabilities vs proof beyond reasonable doubt
Presumption of debt vs proof of company responsibility under s. 141

keyTakeaways: It covers receipt for discharge of debt or other liability.
It does not replace the s. 138 proviso.
It does not decide forum or vicarious liability.
